displayText: Welcome to chess, a game for two players. One player has the light pieces and is called White; the other has the dark pieces and is called Black.

displayText: Each player starts with sixteen pieces. White's are lined up on the two rows nearest to White: eight pawns in front and eight larger pieces behind.

displayText: Black's sixteen pieces stand the same way on the far side, facing White's army across the empty middle of the board.

displayText: White always makes the first move of the game. Here White pushes the pawn in front of the queen two squares forward.

displayText: Then Black answers, pushing the pawn in front of Black's queen two squares forward. After that the turns alternate: White, Black, White, Black, one move at a time.

displayText: On your turn you must make exactly one move. You cannot skip a turn, and you cannot move twice in a row.

displayText: The board has sixty-four squares in eight rows of eight, coloured light and dark. The Chessboard lesson shows how every square gets its name.

displayText: Each army has one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights and eight pawns. Every kind of piece moves in its own way.

displayText: The most important piece is the king. Each king starts in the middle of its back row, right beside its queen, facing the other king.
text: The most important piece is the king. Each king starts in the middle of its back row, right beside its queen, facing the other king.

displayText: Usually, a piece captures by moving onto a square held by an enemy piece, which is then taken off the board. Here White's knight jumps onto a black pawn and captures it.

displayText: Capturing pieces helps, but the real goal is the enemy king. Here White's rook attacks the black king along a straight, open line. An attacked king is said to be in check.
text: Capturing pieces helps, but the real goal is the enemy king. Here White's rook attacks the black king along a straight, open line. An attacked king is said to be in check.

displayText: A king in check must escape at once. This king can step to either side, off the rook's line, so the game goes on.

displayText: Now White's rook slides all the way to the far corner and checks the black king. The king's own pawns block its way forward, and the rook covers the rest of that back row, so there is no escape.

displayText: A king in check with no way out is checkmated. Checkmate ends the game at once, and the player who gives it wins.

displayText: Notice that the king is never actually captured. The game is over the moment it is checkmated, so it never leaves the board.

displayText: Not every game ends in checkmate. A player may resign, which means giving up, and some games end in a draw, where nobody wins.

displayText: Chess grew from a game played in India about fifteen hundred years ago. It spread through Persia to Europe, where the rules we use today settled about five hundred years ago.

displayText: Diagonals come in many lengths. This one has just three squares, f1, g2 and h3, and all three are light.

displayText: The four middle squares are d4, e4, d5 and e5. Together they are called the centre, and you will hear about them often.

displayText: Meet the pawn, the smallest member of each army. Every player starts the game with eight of them.

displayText: White's eight pawns stand on the second rank, from a2 to h2. Black's eight pawns stand on the seventh rank, from a7 to h7.
text: White's eight pawns stand on the second rank, from A two to H two. Black's eight pawns stand on the seventh rank, from A seven to H seven.

displayText: Pawns walk straight ahead, usually one square per move; there is one exception you will see soon. This white pawn steps from g3 to g4.
text: Pawns walk straight ahead, usually one square per move; there is one exception you will see soon. This white pawn steps from G three to G four.

displayText: A pawn can never move backwards or sideways. From g4 its only step is forward, to g5.
text: A pawn can never move backwards or sideways. From G four its only step is forward, to G five.

displayText: For Black, forward means towards the first rank, on White's side. This black pawn steps from b7 to b6.
text: For Black, forward means towards the first rank, on White's side. This black pawn steps from B seven to B six.

displayText: On its very first move, a pawn may go two squares instead of one. This pawn on d2 may step to d3 or go straight to d4.
text: On its very first move, a pawn may go two squares instead of one. This pawn on D two may step to D three or go straight to D four.

displayText: Here it takes the double step, from d2 to d4, passing over the empty square d3.
text: Here it takes the double step, from D two to D four, passing over the empty square D three.

displayText: The double step is a choice, not a rule. This pawn moves just one square, from f2 to f3.
text: The double step is a choice, not a rule. This pawn moves just one square, from F two to F three.

displayText: Now that this pawn has moved, its chance for a double step is gone. From f3 it can only go to f4.
text: Now that this pawn has moved, its chance for a double step is gone. From F three it can only go to F four.

displayText: A pawn cannot jump over anything. The black knight on g3 stands right in front of this pawn, so the pawn cannot move at all.
text: A pawn cannot jump over anything. The black knight on G three stands right in front of this pawn, so the pawn cannot move at all.

displayText: The double step needs both squares empty. This pawn may step to b3, but the black bishop on b4 stops it reaching b4.
text: The double step needs both squares empty. This pawn may step to B three, but the black bishop on B four stops it reaching B four.

displayText: A pawn captures differently from the way it moves: one square diagonally forward. This pawn on g3 attacks the knight on h4.
text: A pawn captures differently from the way it moves: one square diagonally forward. This pawn on G three attacks the knight on H four.

displayText: The pawn takes the knight by moving from g3 to h4. The knight leaves the board, and the pawn stands in its place.
text: The pawn takes the knight by moving from G three to H four. The knight leaves the board, and the pawn stands in its place.

displayText: A pawn attacks the squares just ahead of it on each diagonal. This pawn on f4 attacks e5 and g5.
text: A pawn attacks the squares just ahead of it on each diagonal. This pawn on F four attacks E five and G five.

displayText: A pawn cannot capture straight ahead. These two pawns on c4 and c5 block each other, and neither of them can move.
text: A pawn cannot capture straight ahead. These two pawns on C four and C five block each other, and neither of them can move.

displayText: A blocked pawn can still capture. When a black knight stands on b5, the white pawn takes it by moving from c4 to b5.
text: A blocked pawn can still capture. When a black knight stands on B five, the white pawn takes it by moving from C four to B five.

displayText: Pawns never capture backwards. The knights on c4 and e4 are behind the pawn on d5, so it cannot take them.
text: Pawns never capture backwards. The knights on C four and E four are behind the pawn on D five, so it cannot take them.

displayText: Black's pawns capture diagonally forward too, which for Black means towards the first rank. This black pawn takes the knight, moving from f5 to g4.
text: Black's pawns capture diagonally forward too, which for Black means towards the first rank. This black pawn takes the knight, moving from F five to G four.

displayText: A pawn is worth one point, the smallest value of any piece. Yet pawns standing side by side, or guarding each other, are hard to get past.

displayText: Pawn Duel is a game played with pawns alone. It is a fun way to practise moving and capturing with pawns.
text: Pawn Duel is a game played with pawns alone. It is a fun way to practise moving and capturing with pawns.

displayText: Each side has six pawns. White's stand from b2 to g2, and Black's stand from b7 to g7.
text: Each side has six pawns. White's stand from B two to G two, and Black's stand from B seven to G seven.

displayText: White moves first, and the players take turns. Pawns move as usual, so White's pawn makes a double step from e2 to e4.
text: White moves first, and the players take turns. Pawns move as usual, so White's pawn makes a double step from E two to E four.

displayText: Black answers with a double step too, from d7 to d5. Now the two pawns attack each other.
text: Black answers with a double step too, from D seven to D five. Now the two pawns attack each other.

displayText: Pawns capture diagonally, just as in a real game. White's pawn takes on d5, moving from e4 to d5.
text: Pawns capture diagonally, just as in a real game. White's pawn takes on D five, moving from E four to D five.

displayText: The first way to win is to reach the far rank. This white pawn on c7 is one step from c8. If it gets there, White wins at once.
text: The first way to win is to reach the far rank. This white pawn on C seven is one step from C eight. If it gets there, White wins at once.

displayText: Black aims the other way. A black pawn that reaches the first rank wins the game, so this pawn on f2 needs just one more step.
text: Black aims the other way. A black pawn that reaches the first rank wins the game, so this pawn on F two needs just one more step.

displayText: The second way is to capture every opposing pawn. White takes Black's last pawn, moving from d5 to e6. Every black pawn is now gone, and the game goes to White.
text: The second way is to capture every opposing pawn. White takes Black's last pawn, moving from D five to E six. Every black pawn is now gone, and the game goes to White.

displayText: The third way: your opponent has no move on their turn. White's pawn steps from b4 to b5.
text: The third way: your opponent has no move on their turn. White's pawn steps from B four to B five.

displayText: Now both black pawns are blocked, and nothing stands diagonally in front of them to capture. Black has no move, so White wins.
text: Now both black pawns are blocked, and nothing stands diagonally in front of them to capture. Black has no move, so White wins.

displayText: In Pawn Duel a pawn never turns into another piece, and one special pawn capture is left out. You will meet both in Promotion and En Passant.
text: In Pawn Duel a pawn never turns into another piece, and one special pawn capture is left out. You will meet both in Promotion and En Passant.

displayText: Look before you push. If this white pawn moves to e5, the black pawn on d6 can capture it.
text: Look before you push. If this white pawn moves to E five, the black pawn on D six can capture it.

displayText: A pawn guarded by another pawn is hard to win. If Black's pawn on e5 takes on d4, the pawn on c3 takes it back.
text: A pawn guarded by another pawn is hard to win. If Black's pawn on E five takes on D four, the pawn on C three takes it back.

displayText: When two pawns race, count the steps. White's pawn on g4 needs four moves to reach g8, and Black's pawn on b6 needs five to reach b1.

displayText: This tall piece with a notched top, like a castle tower, is the rook. Each player begins with two rooks in the corners, with the king between them: White's on a1 and h1, Black's on a8 and h8.
text: This tall piece with a notched top, like a castle tower, is the rook. Each player begins with two rooks in the corners, with the king between them: White's on A one and H one, Black's on A eight and H eight.

displayText: The rook moves in straight lines. It can go up or down its file, or sideways along its rank.
text: The rook moves in straight lines. It can go up or down its file, or sideways along its rank.

displayText: It may travel as far as it likes in one move. Here the rook slides from c5 all the way along the rank to h5.
text: It may travel as far as it likes in one move. Here the rook slides from C five all the way along the rank to H five.

displayText: Back on c5, let's count every square the rook could reach in one move. There are fourteen of them.
text: Back on C five, let's count every square the rook could reach in one move. There are fourteen of them.

displayText: On an empty board, the rook reaches fourteen squares from any square at all, even from a corner like h8: seven down the file and seven along the rank.
text: On an empty board, the rook reaches fourteen squares from any square at all, even from a corner like H eight: seven down the file and seven along the rank.

displayText: The rook never moves diagonally. The four squares touching c5 at the corners are out of its reach in one move.
text: The rook never moves diagonally. The four squares touching C five at the corners are out of its reach in one move.

displayText: The rook cannot jump over anything. White's own pawn on d6 blocks the file, so d7 and d8 are out of reach.
text: The rook cannot jump over anything. White's own pawn on D six blocks the file, so D seven and D eight are out of reach.

displayText: The pawn on f4 does the same along the rank. The rook can stop on e4, but g4 and h4 are behind the pawn.
text: The pawn on F four does the same along the rank. The rook can stop on E four, but G four and H four are behind the pawn.

displayText: A rook can never land on a square held by its own side. To this rook, the white pawns are walls, not targets.
text: A rook can never land on a square held by its own side. To this rook, the white pawns are walls, not targets.

displayText: The rook captures the same way it moves. Here it can reach Black's knight on d7 and Black's pawn on g4.
text: The rook captures the same way it moves. Here it can reach Black's knight on D seven and Black's pawn on G four.

displayText: The rook moves from d4 to d7 and takes the knight's place. The captured knight leaves the board for good.
text: The rook moves from D four to D seven and takes the knight's place. The captured knight leaves the board for good.

displayText: A rook can capture only the first enemy piece in its line. The rook on a1 can take the pawn on a5, but the queen on a8, behind that pawn, is out of reach.
text: A rook can capture only the first enemy piece in its line. The rook on A one can take the pawn on A five, but the queen on A eight, behind that pawn, is out of reach.

displayText: Rooks love open lines. The rook on d1 sees all the way up the empty d-file, while the rook on a1 is blocked by its own pawn on a2 and can only shuffle along the first rank.
text: Rooks love open lines. The rook on D one sees all the way up the empty d-file, while the rook on A one is blocked by its own pawn on A two and can only shuffle along the first rank.

displayText: Two rooks on the same rank or file, with nothing between them, guard each other. If one is captured, the other can take back.
text: Two rooks on the same rank or file, with nothing between them, guard each other. If one is captured, the other can take back.

displayText: A rook is worth five points, as much as five pawns. Of the pieces that are counted in points, only the queen is worth more.
text: A rook is worth five points, as much as five pawns. Of the pieces that are counted in points, only the queen is worth more.

displayText: So check before you capture. The rook could take the pawn on d5, but Black's pawn on e6 would then capture the rook: five points lost for one.
text: So check before you capture. The rook could take the pawn on D five, but Black's pawn on E six would then capture the rook: five points lost for one.

displayText: The rook moves in straight lines, any distance, never through pieces. It captures by landing on an enemy piece, and it is worth five points.
text: The rook moves in straight lines, any distance, never through pieces. It captures by landing on an enemy piece, and it is worth five points.

displayText: One way to win is to capture every opposing piece, rooks and pawns alike. A side with no move on its turn loses.

displayText: Meet the bishop, the piece with a pointed, slanted top. Each player starts with two, either side of the queen and king: White's on c1 and f1, Black's on c8 and f8.

displayText: A king in check cannot escape by stepping away along the checking line. If the king left d4 for e4, d4 would no longer block the rook, so e4 would be attacked too. Both c4 and e4 are unsafe.
text: A king in check cannot escape by stepping away along the checking line. If the king left D four for E four, D four would no longer block the rook, so E four would be attacked too. Both C four and E four are unsafe.

displayText: An enemy piece is only safe to capture if nothing protects it. The bishop on h6 guards the knight on f4, so f4 is not a safe square for the king.

displayText: Now let's plan a walk. The white king on d2 wants to reach f6, but Black's rook and knight guard many squares on the way.

displayText: First, mark every empty square the black pieces attack. The rook covers the fifth rank and the d-file above the pawn, the knight covers squares such as e4, f3 and h3, and the black king guards the squares around it.

displayText: The white pawn on d3 blocks the rook's file. That is why d2, where the king stands, is safe.
text: The white pawn on D three blocks the rook's file. That is why D two, where the king stands, is safe.

displayText: Now look along the fifth rank. The rook protects the knight on g5, so the king cannot take it. The only empty safe square on that rank is h5.
text: Now look along the fifth rank. The rook protects the knight on G five, so the king cannot take it. The only empty safe square on that rank is H five.

displayText: So the route bends: e3, f4 and g4, then through the gap at h5, and back across to g6 and f6. Every one of those squares is safe.
text: So the route bends: E three, F four and G four, then through the gap at H five, and back across to G six and F six. Every one of those squares is safe.

displayText: The king steps from d2 to e3. Then it steps from e3 to f4. Then it steps from f4 to g4.

displayText: Next the king slips from g4 to h5. Then it steps from h5 to g6. Finally it steps from g6 to f6 and has arrived.
text: Next the king slips from G four to H five. Then it steps from H five to G six. Finally it steps from G six to F six and has arrived.

displayText: The aim of chess is checkmate. To understand it, we first need a closer look at check.
text: The aim of chess is checkmate. To understand it, we first need a closer look at check.

displayText: Check means the king is attacked. The black rook on e7 attacks the white king on e1, so White is in check.
text: Check means the king is attacked. The black rook on E seven attacks the white king on E one, so White is in check.

displayText: A side in check must get out of it on the very next move. You may never make a move that leaves your own king attacked.
text: A side in check must get out of it on the very next move. You may never make a move that leaves your own king attacked.

displayText: You can answer a check in three ways. Step the king to safety, put a piece in the way, or take the attacker.
text: You can answer a check in three ways. Step the king to safety, put a piece in the way, or take the attacker.

displayText: First way: move the king to a safe square. From e1 it can go to d1, d2, f1 or f2, but not to e2, which is still on the rook's file.
text: First way: move the king to a safe square. From E one it can go to D one, D two, F one or F two, but not to E two, which is still on the rook's file.

displayText: The king steps from e1 to d2. Nothing attacks it there, so the check is over.
text: The king steps from E one to D two. Nothing attacks it there, so the check is over.

displayText: Second way: put a piece in between. The rook on a1 checks the king on g1, and the king has no safe square to go to.
text: Second way: put a piece in between. The rook on A one checks the king on G one, and the king has no safe square to go to.

displayText: The bishop steps from e2 to f1, between the rook and the king. The rook's line now stops at the bishop, so the check is blocked.
text: The bishop steps from E two to F one, between the rook and the king. The rook's line now stops at the bishop, so the check is blocked.

displayText: Third way: capture the piece giving check. The knight on d3 checks the king on e1, and a knight's check can never be blocked, because knights jump.
text: Third way: capture the piece giving check. The knight on D three checks the king on E one, and a knight's check can never be blocked, because knights jump.

displayText: The pawn on c2 captures the knight on d3, and the check is over.
text: The pawn on C two captures the knight on D three, and the check is over.

displayText: Checkmate is a check with no way out: the king cannot escape, nothing can block, and nothing can capture the checking piece. The game ends at once.
text: Checkmate is a check with no way out: the king cannot escape, nothing can block, and nothing can capture the checking piece. The game ends at once.

displayText: Black's rook swoops down from a8 to a1. Now the white king on g1 is in check.
text: Black's rook swoops down from A eight to A one. Now the white king on G one is in check.

displayText: The king cannot step to f1 or h1, which the rook attacks, and its own pawns fill f2, g2 and h2. No white piece can block or capture. Checkmate: Black wins.
text: The king cannot step to F one or H one, which the rook attacks, and its own pawns fill F two, G two and H two. No white piece can block or capture. Checkmate: Black wins.

displayText: The queen and king make a strong team. The queen slides from h7 to e7, right in front of the black king, and the white king on e6 protects her.
text: The queen and king make a strong team. The queen slides from H seven to E seven, right in front of the black king, and the white king on E six protects her.

displayText: The queen attacks d8, f8, d7 and f7. The black king cannot capture her either, because the white king guards her. Checkmate.
text: The queen attacks D eight, F eight, D seven and F seven. The black king cannot capture her either, because the white king guards her. Checkmate.

displayText: A rook can checkmate a king that is stuck on the edge. The white rook rushes up from h1 to h8, giving check along the eighth rank.
text: A rook can checkmate a king that is stuck on the edge. The white rook rushes up from H one to H eight, giving check along the eighth rank.

displayText: The rook's line covers b8 and d8, and the white king on c6 guards b7, c7 and d7. The black king has nowhere to go, so this is checkmate.
text: The rook's line covers B eight and D eight, and the white king on C six guards B seven, C seven and D seven. The black king has nowhere to go, so this is checkmate.

displayText: Compare this board, with the white king on c5. The same rook move to h8 gives check, but now the black king can step out to b7, c7 or d7.
text: Compare this board, with the white king on C five. The same rook move to H eight gives check, but now the black king can step out to B seven, C seven or D seven.

displayText: Check: the king is attacked, so answer it by moving, blocking or capturing. Checkmate: a check with no answer, and the game is over.
text: Check: the king is attacked, so answer it by moving, blocking or capturing. Checkmate: a check with no answer, and the game is over.

displayText: Every game starts from the same position. Let's set up the board together, beginning with White's pieces.
text: Every game starts from the same position. Let's set up the board together, beginning with White's pieces.

displayText: First, turn the board so each player has a light square in the right-hand corner nearest to them. For White that square is h1; for Black it is a8.
text: First, turn the board so each player has a light square in the right-hand corner nearest to them. For White that square is H one; for Black it is A eight.

displayText: White's two rooks go in White's corners, on a1 and h1.
text: White's two rooks go in White's corners, on A one and H one.

displayText: Next to each rook goes a knight, so White's knights stand on b1 and g1.
text: Next to each rook goes a knight, so White's knights stand on B one and G one.

displayText: Beside each knight goes a bishop. White's bishops stand on c1 and f1.
text: Beside each knight goes a bishop. White's bishops stand on C one and F one.

displayText: Two squares are still empty in the middle of White's back row: d1 and e1.
text: Two squares are still empty in the middle of White's back row: D one and E one.

displayText: The queen goes on the square of her own colour. White's queen is light, so she stands on d1, which is a light square.
text: The queen goes on the square of her own colour. White's queen is light, so she stands on D one, which is a light square.

displayText: The king takes the last square, right beside his queen. White's king stands on e1.
text: The king takes the last square, right beside his queen. White's king stands on E one.

displayText: From a1 to h1, White's back row now holds a rook, a knight, a bishop, the queen, the king, a bishop, a knight and a rook.
text: From A one to H one, White's back row now holds a rook, a knight, a bishop, the queen, the king, a bishop, a knight and a rook.

displayText: Black's back row mirrors White's. Black's rooks stand on a8 and h8, the knights on b8 and g8, and the bishops on c8 and f8.
text: Black's back row mirrors White's. Black's rooks stand on A eight and H eight, the knights on B eight and G eight, and the bishops on C eight and F eight.

displayText: Black's queen is dark, so she goes on the dark square d8. Now the two queens face each other along the d-file.
text: Black's queen is dark, so she goes on the dark square D eight. Now the two queens face each other along the d-file.

displayText: Black's king goes beside his queen on e8. In front of them, Black's eight pawns fill the seventh rank.
text: Black's king goes beside his queen on E eight. In front of them, Black's eight pawns fill the seventh rank.

displayText: Last of all, White's eight pawns fill the second rank. The board is ready.
text: Last of all, White's eight pawns fill the second rank. The board is ready.

displayText: Each piece faces the same kind of piece along its file. Rook faces rook, queen faces queen, and king faces king.
text: Each piece faces the same kind of piece along its file. Rook faces rook, queen faces queen, and king faces king.

displayText: Before you play, check two things. Is the corner square on each player's right light? Is each queen on a square of her own colour?
text: Before you play, check two things. Is the corner square on each player's right light? Is each queen on a square of her own colour?

displayText: A common mistake is to swap the king and queen. Here the white queen stands on e1, a dark square, so this setup is wrong.
text: A common mistake is to swap the king and queen. Here the white queen stands on E one, a dark square, so this setup is wrong.

displayText: Swap them back. Now the white queen is on d1, her own light square, with the king beside her on e1.
text: Swap them back. Now the white queen is on D one, her own light square, with the king beside her on E one.

displayText: Another slip is mixing up the knights and bishops. Here White's bishops stand on b1 and g1, next to the rooks, which is wrong.
text: Another slip is mixing up the knights and bishops. Here White's bishops stand on B one and G one, next to the rooks, which is wrong.

displayText: Remember the order from each corner: rook, knight, bishop. With the knights on b1 and g1 and the bishops on c1 and f1, White's side is right again.
text: Remember the order from each corner: rook, knight, bishop. With the knights on B one and G one and the bishops on C one and F one, White's side is right again.

displayText: Every piece is in place. White moves first, so once the board is set, White begins.
text: Every piece is in place. White moves first, so once the board is set, White begins.

displayText: Castling is a special move made by the king and a rook together. It is the only move in chess where you move two of your pieces at once.
text: Castling is a special move made by the king and a rook together. It is the only move in chess where you move two of your pieces at once.

displayText: To castle on the kingside, the king moves two squares towards the h1 rook, from e1 to g1. Then the rook jumps over the king, from h1 to f1.
text: To castle on the kingside, the king moves two squares towards the H one rook, from E one to G one. Then the rook jumps over the king, from H one to F one.

displayText: Now the king stands on g1, near the corner, and the rook stands right beside it on f1.
text: Now the king stands on G one, near the corner, and the rook stands right beside it on F one.

displayText: Queenside castling works the same way. The king moves two squares towards the a1 rook, from e1 to c1. Then the rook jumps over the king, from a1 to d1.
text: Queenside castling works the same way. The king moves two squares towards the A one rook, from E one to C one. Then the rook jumps over the king, from A one to D one.

displayText: Either way, the king always moves exactly two squares, and the rook lands right next to the king, on its other side.
text: Either way, the king always moves exactly two squares, and the rook lands right next to the king, on its other side.

displayText: Black castles in the same way. The king moves from e8 to g8. Then the rook jumps from h8 to f8.
text: Black castles in the same way. The king moves from E eight to G eight. Then the rook jumps from H eight to F eight.

displayText: Now Black castles on the queenside. The king travels from e8 to c8. Then the rook hops from a8 to d8.
text: Now Black castles on the queenside. The king travels from E eight to C eight. Then the rook hops from A eight to D eight.

displayText: Kingside castling is often called short castling, and queenside castling long castling, because the queenside rook travels further.
text: Kingside castling is often called short castling, and queenside castling long castling, because the queenside rook travels further.

displayText: Why castle? A king in the middle is in danger once pawns leave the centre. Here the d-file is open, with no pawns on it, and the black rook on d8 controls it, right beside the white king.
text: Why castle? A king in the middle is in danger once pawns leave the centre. Here the d-file is open, with no pawns on it, and the black rook on D eight controls it, right beside the white king.

displayText: So White castles. First the king slides across from e1 to g1. Then the rook hops over it from h1 to f1. Now the king sits behind the pawns on f2, g2 and h2, away from the open files.
text: So White castles. First the king slides across from E one to G one. Then the rook hops over it from H one to F one. Now the king sits behind the pawns on F two, G two and H two, away from the open files.

displayText: Castling also brings the rook towards the centre quickly. From f1 it can move straight to the open e-file or d-file.
text: Castling also brings the rook towards the centre quickly. From F one it can move straight to the open e-file or d-file.

displayText: Queenside castling brings the rook to the centre at once. First the king slides across from e1 to c1. Then the rook hops over it from a1 to d1, onto a central file.
text: Queenside castling brings the rook to the centre at once. First the king slides across from E one to C one. Then the rook hops over it from A one to D one, onto a central file.

displayText: Castling needs a clear road between king and rook. Here the knight and bishop have already come out, so f1 and g1 are free.
text: Castling needs a clear road between king and rook. Here the knight and bishop have already come out, so F one and G one are free.

displayText: Castling early, once your knight and bishop have moved out, is a good habit. The exact conditions come in Castling Rules.
text: Castling early, once your knight and bishop have moved out, is a good habit. The exact conditions come in Castling Rules.

displayText: On a real board, move the king two squares first, then lift the rook over it, using the same hand. Moving the king first shows clearly that you are castling.
text: On a real board, move the king two squares first, then lift the rook over it, using the same hand. Moving the king first shows clearly that you are castling.

displayText: Now try it yourself. In this position, castle to tuck your king behind its pawns and bring your rook towards the centre.
text: Now try it yourself. In this position, castle to tuck your king behind its pawns and bring your rook towards the centre.

displayText: Castling is a powerful move, so it comes with strict rules. Check every one of them before you castle.
text: Castling is a powerful move, so it comes with strict rules. Check every one of them before you castle.

displayText: First, nothing may stand between the king and the rook. The bishop on f1 and the knight on g1 are in the way, so White cannot castle on the kingside yet.
text: First, nothing may stand between the king and the rook. The bishop on F one and the knight on G one are in the way, so White cannot castle on the kingside yet.

displayText: The knight leaps out from g1 to f3. Then the bishop heads off from f1 to c4. Now f1 and g1 are both empty, and the path is clear.
text: The knight leaps out from G one to F three. Then the bishop heads off from F one to C four. Now F one and G one are both empty, and the path is clear.

displayText: On the queenside, three squares must be empty: b1, c1 and d1. Here the knight on b1 is still in the way, so queenside castling must wait.
text: On the queenside, three squares must be empty: B one, C one and D one. Here the knight on B one is still in the way, so queenside castling must wait.

displayText: Second, the king must never have moved. Here the king steps from e1 to f1. Later it steps back from f1 to e1.
text: Second, the king must never have moved. Here the king steps from E one to F one. Later it steps back from F one to E one.

displayText: It looks just as before, but this king has moved. It can never castle again, on either side, for the rest of the game.
text: It looks just as before, but this king has moved. It can never castle again, on either side, for the rest of the game.

displayText: Third, the rook must never have moved either. The rook goes from h1 to h3. Later it comes back from h3 to h1.
text: Third, the rook must never have moved either. The rook goes from H one to H three. Later it comes back from H three to H one.

displayText: White can never castle with this h1 rook now. But the a1 rook and the king have stayed at home, so queenside castling is still possible.
text: White can never castle with this H one rook now. But the A one rook and the king have stayed at home, so queenside castling is still possible.

displayText: Fourth, you cannot castle while your king is in check. The bishop on b4 attacks the king on e1, so White must answer the check another way.
text: Fourth, you cannot castle while your king is in check. The bishop on B four attacks the king on E one, so White must answer the check another way.

displayText: Fifth, the king may not cross an attacked square. The bishop on c4 attacks f1, the square the king passes over, so kingside castling is not allowed.
text: Fifth, the king may not cross an attacked square. The bishop on C four attacks F one, the square the king passes over, so kingside castling is not allowed.

displayText: Sixth, the king may not land in check. The rook on g6 attacks g1 down the open g-file, so the king cannot castle onto it.
text: Sixth, the king may not land in check. The rook on G six attacks G one down the open g-file, so the king cannot castle onto it.

displayText: These check rules only matter at the moment you castle. The black rook moves from g6 to a6, and now nothing attacks e1, f1 or g1, so White may castle.
text: These check rules only matter at the moment you castle. The black rook moves from G six to A six, and now nothing attacks E one, F one or G one, so White may castle.

displayText: On the queenside the king crosses d1 and lands on c1, so those squares must be safe. But b1 is different: only the rook passes over it, so it may be attacked.
text: On the queenside the king crosses D one and lands on C one, so those squares must be safe. But B one is different: only the rook passes over it, so it may be attacked.

displayText: So White may castle here. First the king slides across from e1 to c1. Then the rook hops over it from a1 to d1, straight across the attacked b1 square.
text: So White may castle here. First the king slides across from E one to C one. Then the rook hops over it from A one to D one, straight across the attacked B one square.

displayText: The same holds for Black. The bishop on e5 attacks b8, but c8, d8 and e8 are safe, so Black may still castle on the queenside.
text: The same holds for Black. The bishop on E five attacks B eight, but C eight, D eight and E eight are safe, so Black may still castle on the queenside.

displayText: Before castling, ask: is the path empty? Have the king and this rook stayed at home? Is the king safe now, on the way and where it lands? If every answer is yes, you may castle.
text: Before castling, ask: is the path empty? Have the king and this rook stayed at home? Is the king safe now, on the way and where it lands? If every answer is yes, you may castle.

displayText: Pawns have two special rules. Promotion rewards a pawn that marches all the way, and en passant is a surprising capture.
text: Pawns have two special rules. Promotion rewards a pawn that marches all the way, and en passant is a surprising capture.

displayText: This white pawn steps from b6 to b7. Now it is one square from the eighth rank, the far end of the board.
text: This white pawn steps from B six to B seven. Now it is one square from the eighth rank, the far end of the board.

displayText: The pawn steps to b8 and is changed at once into a queen. This is called promotion.
text: The pawn steps to B eight and is changed at once into a queen. This is called promotion.

displayText: The player picks the new piece: a queen, rook, bishop or knight, always of the pawn's own colour. Turning into a king is never allowed, and neither is remaining a pawn.
text: The player picks the new piece: a queen, rook, bishop or knight, always of the pawn's own colour. Turning into a king is never allowed, and neither is remaining a pawn.

displayText: Most players choose a queen, the strongest piece. You may promote even while your first queen is still on the board: this pawn becomes a queen on g8, so White now has two queens.
text: Most players choose a queen, the strongest piece. You may promote even while your first queen is still on the board: this pawn becomes a queen on G eight, so White now has two queens.

displayText: Black's pawns promote when they reach the first rank. This black pawn steps from f2 to f1 and becomes a black queen.
text: Black's pawns promote when they reach the first rank. This black pawn steps from F two to F one and becomes a black queen.

displayText: A pawn can also promote by capturing. The way ahead to c8 is blocked, so this pawn takes the rook on d8 and becomes a queen there.
text: A pawn can also promote by capturing. The way ahead to C eight is blocked, so this pawn takes the rook on D eight and becomes a queen there.

displayText: Sometimes a knight is the better choice. This pawn on f7 is about to reach f8.
text: Sometimes a knight is the better choice. This pawn on F seven is about to reach F eight.

displayText: It becomes a knight on f8. The knight attacks the black king on e6 and the black queen on h7 at the same time. A queen on f8 would attack neither.
text: It becomes a knight on F eight. The knight attacks the black king on E six and the black queen on H seven at the same time. A queen on F eight would attack neither.

displayText: The black king must move out of check, and here it steps from e6 to e5. Then White's knight takes the queen, moving from f8 to h7.
text: The black king must move out of check, and here it steps from E six to E five. Then White's knight takes the queen, moving from F eight to H seven.

displayText: Now the second rule. A white pawn stands on f5, and a black pawn waits on g7, still on its starting square.
text: Now the second rule. A white pawn stands on F five, and a black pawn waits on G seven, still on its starting square.

displayText: Black's pawn makes a double step, from g7 to g5. It lands right beside the white pawn.
text: Black's pawn makes a double step, from G seven to G five. It lands right beside the white pawn.

displayText: Had it stepped only to g6, the white pawn could have captured it there. With its double step, it tried to slip past.
text: Had it stepped only to G six, the white pawn could have captured it there. With its double step, it tried to slip past.

displayText: White may capture it anyway, as if it had moved one square. White's pawn moves from f5 to g6, and the black pawn on g5 is taken off the board.
text: White may capture it anyway, as if it had moved one square. White's pawn moves from F five to G six, and the black pawn on G five is taken off the board.

displayText: The name en passant is French and means in passing. Only pawns can make this capture, and only pawns can be taken this way.
text: The name en passant is French and means in passing. Only pawns can make this capture, and only pawns can be taken this way.

displayText: En passant must be played at once. Black's pawn makes a double step, from g7 to g5. White's pawn moves from h2 to h3 instead.
text: En passant must be played at once. Black's pawn makes a double step, from G seven to G five. White's pawn moves from H two to H three instead.

displayText: Black's pawn moves from b7 to b6. The chance is gone for good: the pawn on f5 can no longer capture the pawn on g5.
text: Black's pawn moves from B seven to B six. The chance is gone for good: the pawn on F five can no longer capture the pawn on G five.

displayText: This black pawn steps one square, from g6 to g5. It did not make a double step, so en passant is not allowed here.
text: This black pawn steps one square, from G six to G five. It did not make a double step, so en passant is not allowed here.

displayText: Black can capture en passant too. White's pawn makes a double step, from b2 to b4. Black's pawn on c4 captures it in passing by moving to b3.
text: Black can capture en passant too. White's pawn makes a double step, from B two to B four. Black's pawn on C four captures it in passing by moving to B three.

displayText: Now try both rules. Black's pawn has just made a double step to d5. Capture it en passant, then race a pawn to the eighth rank and promote it.
text: Now try both rules. Black's pawn has just made a double step to D five. Capture it en passant, then race a pawn to the eighth rank and promote it.

displayText: Not every chess game has a winner. When a game is drawn, nobody wins, and in a tournament each player usually scores half a point.
text: Not every chess game has a winner. When a game is drawn, nobody wins, and in a tournament each player usually scores half a point.

displayText: A game can be drawn in five main ways: stalemate, not enough pieces to checkmate, repeating a position, a long run of moves with no capture or pawn move, and agreement.
text: A game can be drawn in five main ways: stalemate, not enough pieces to checkmate, repeating a position, a long run of moves with no capture or pawn move, and agreement.

displayText: Here Black has only a king left, while White has a king and a queen. White should win, but must be careful.
text: Here Black has only a king left, while White has a king and a queen. White should win, but must be careful.

displayText: White's queen moves from c5 to c7. Now it is Black's turn.
text: White's queen moves from C five to C seven. Now it is Black's turn.

displayText: Black's king on a8 is not in check. But the queen attacks a7, b7 and b8, so the king has nowhere to go, and Black has no other piece to move.
text: Black's king on A eight is not in check. But the queen attacks A seven, B seven and B eight, so the king has nowhere to go, and Black has no other piece to move.

displayText: This is stalemate. When the player to move is not in check but has no legal move, the game ends at once as a draw.
text: This is stalemate. When the player to move is not in check but has no legal move, the game ends at once as a draw.

displayText: How is this different from checkmate? A checkmated king is attacked and has no escape. Here the king is not attacked at all; Black simply has no move to play.
text: How is this different from checkmate? A checkmated king is attacked and has no escape. Here the king is not attacked at all; Black simply has no move to play.

displayText: Stalemate can happen with other pieces still on the board. If it is Black's turn here, the pawn on a5 is blocked by White's pawn on a4, and every square around the king is attacked.
text: Stalemate can happen with other pieces still on the board. If it is Black's turn here, the pawn on A five is blocked by White's pawn on A four, and every square around the king is attacked.

displayText: Black's king on h8 is not in check, and Black has no legal move, so this is stalemate too. When you are winning, make sure each move leaves your opponent a legal move, unless your move is checkmate.
text: Black's king on H eight is not in check, and Black has no legal move, so this is stalemate too. When you are winning, make sure each move leaves your opponent a legal move, unless your move is checkmate.

displayText: A game is also drawn when neither side can possibly give checkmate. With only two kings left, checkmate can never happen, so the game is over.
text: A game is also drawn when neither side can possibly give checkmate. With only two kings left, checkmate can never happen, so the game is over.

displayText: A king and one bishop cannot checkmate a lone king, and neither can a king and one knight. These games are drawn as well.
text: A king and one bishop cannot checkmate a lone king, and neither can a king and one knight. These games are drawn as well.

displayText: A single pawn is a different story. It might reach the last rank and become a queen, so the game goes on.
text: A single pawn is a different story. It might reach the last rank and become a queen, so the game goes on.

displayText: Now a draw by repetition. Black has two rooks and a knight against White's queen, so Black is ahead. White's best hope is to keep giving check.
text: Now a draw by repetition. Black has two rooks and a knight against White's queen, so Black is ahead. White's best hope is to keep giving check.

displayText: White's queen moves from d7 to e8, giving check. Black's king steps from g8 to h7. Remember this position.
text: White's queen moves from D seven to E eight, giving check. Black's king steps from G eight to H seven. Remember this position.

displayText: White's queen checks from e4. Black's king goes back to g8. White's queen checks from e8 again. Black's king returns to h7. The same position has appeared a second time.
text: White's queen checks from E four. Black's king goes back to G eight. White's queen checks from E eight again. Black's king returns to H seven. The same position has appeared a second time.

displayText: White's queen checks from e4. Black's king goes to g8. White's queen checks from e8. Black's king goes to h7. This is the third time.
text: White's queen checks from E four. Black's king goes to G eight. White's queen checks from E eight. Black's king goes to H seven. This is the third time.

displayText: A position counts as repeated only if the same side is to move and the same moves are available, castling included. After three such repeats, the player to move can claim a draw, even if they were not in a row.
text: A position counts as repeated only if the same side is to move and the same moves are available, castling included. After three such repeats, the player to move can claim a draw, even if they were not in a row.

displayText: If nobody claims, play goes on. But if the same position appears five times, the game is drawn automatically.
text: If nobody claims, play goes on. But if the same position appears five times, the game is drawn automatically.

displayText: Another rule stops endless games. If each player makes fifty moves with no capture and no pawn move, the player whose turn it is may claim a draw.
text: Another rule stops endless games. If each player makes fifty moves with no capture and no pawn move, the player whose turn it is may claim a draw.

displayText: After seventy-five moves each with no capture and no pawn move, the game is drawn automatically, unless the last move gave checkmate.
text: After seventy-five moves each with no capture and no pawn move, the game is drawn automatically, unless the last move gave checkmate.

displayText: Finally, once both have made a move, the players can agree to a draw, though some events limit this. Offer it just after making your move; your opponent may accept, or decline by playing on.
text: Finally, once both have made a move, the players can agree to a draw, though some events limit this. Offer it just after making your move; your opponent may accept, or decline by playing on.

displayText: So a game can end in a draw by stalemate, not enough material, repetition, the fifty-move rule or agreement. A draw is half a point: much better than a loss.

displayText: Some pieces are stronger than others. To compare them quickly, chess players give each piece a value in points.
text: Some pieces are stronger than others. To compare them quickly, chess players give each piece a value in points.

displayText: A pawn is worth one point. It is the smallest unit, so the other values are counted in pawns.
text: A pawn is worth one point. It is the smallest unit, so the other values are counted in pawns.

displayText: A knight is worth three points, about the same as three pawns.
text: A knight is worth three points, about the same as three pawns.

displayText: A bishop is also worth three points. Knights and bishops are called minor pieces, and they are roughly equal.
text: A bishop is also worth three points. Knights and bishops are called minor pieces, and they are roughly equal.

displayText: A rook is worth five points, more than a knight or a bishop.
text: A rook is worth five points, more than a knight or a bishop.

displayText: The queen is worth nine points. She combines the moves of a rook and a bishop, so she is the strongest piece.
text: The queen is worth nine points. She combines the moves of a rook and a bishop, so she is the strongest piece.

displayText: The king has no point value. It can never be traded or captured, and if your king is checkmated, you lose the game.
text: The king has no point value. It can never be traded or captured, and if your king is checkmated, you lose the game.

displayText: At the start, each side has eight pawns, two knights, two bishops, two rooks and a queen. Add them up and each army is worth 39 points.
text: At the start, each side has eight pawns, two knights, two bishops, two rooks and a queen. Add them up and each army is worth 39 points.

displayText: Values help you judge trades. Here White can capture the knight on c6, and Black can capture back.

displayText: Each side gave up three points. That is an even trade: nobody gained anything.

displayText: Here White's rook can take the knight on d5, but Black's pawn on e6 guards it.
text: Here White's rook can take the knight on D five, but Black's pawn on E six guards it.

displayText: White's rook captures the knight on d5. Black's pawn captures the rook. White gave five points and got only three back, losing two.
text: White's rook captures the knight on D five. Black's pawn captures the rook. White gave five points and got only three back, losing two.

displayText: This time White's knight can take a rook on e5 that is guarded by the pawn on d6.
text: This time White's knight can take a rook on E five that is guarded by the pawn on D six.

displayText: White's knight captures the rook on e5. Black's pawn captures the knight. White gave three points and won five, gaining two points in the trade.
text: White's knight captures the rook on E five. Black's pawn captures the knight. White gave three points and won five, gaining two points in the trade.

displayText: Look at this position. Black has a whole extra queen, nine points more than White. But it is White's turn.
text: Look at this position. Black has a whole extra queen, nine points more than White. But it is White's turn.

displayText: White's rook moves from e1 to e8. It is checkmate: the king cannot escape, and nothing can block or capture the rook.
text: White's rook moves from E one to E eight. It is checkmate: the king cannot escape, and nothing can block or capture the rook.

displayText: So use piece values to judge trades and captures, but always look for checks and checkmates first. Checkmate decides the game, not points.
text: So use piece values to judge trades and captures, but always look for checks and checkmates first. Checkmate decides the game, not points.

displayText: During a game it helps to know who has more material: more pieces, by value. You find out by counting points.
text: During a game it helps to know who has more material: more pieces, by value. You find out by counting points.

displayText: Start with White. A queen is nine, a rook five, a knight three, and five pawns make five more. White has 22 points.
text: Start with White. A queen is nine, a rook five, a knight three, and five pawns make five more. White has 22 points.

displayText: Now Black. Two rooks make ten, a bishop and a knight add six, and five pawns add five. Black has 21 points.
text: Now Black. Two rooks make ten, a bishop and a knight add six, and five pawns add five. Black has 21 points.

displayText: White has one point more: White is a pawn ahead. Kings are never counted, because each side always has one.

displayText: Counting also shows whether a trade is fair. Here Black is five points ahead, and White's rook can take the rook on d8.

displayText: White's rook captures the rook on d8. Black's rook on f8 captures back on d8.

displayText: Each side lost five points, so the trade was fair. Black was five points ahead before it and is still five points ahead.
text: Each side lost five points, so the trade was fair. Black was five points ahead before it and is still five points ahead.

displayText: Here White's bishop can take the pawn on f7, but Black's king guards that pawn.

text: White's bishop captures the pawn on F seven, giving check. Black's king captures the bishop.

displayText: White gave up three points to win one, so the trade lost two points. White was three points ahead before it, and now only one.
text: White gave up three points to win one, so the trade lost two points. White was three points ahead before it, and now only one.

displayText: Before you capture, count. White's knight attacks the pawn on e5, and Black's knight on c6 defends it: one attacker, one defender.
text: Before you capture, count. White's knight attacks the pawn on E five, and Black's knight on C six defends it: one attacker, one defender.

displayText: White's knight captures the pawn on e5. Black's knight captures the knight. White gave three points for one.
text: White's knight captures the pawn on E five. Black's knight captures the knight. White gave three points for one.

displayText: Now White has a rook on e1 as well. Two white pieces attack the pawn on e5, and only one black piece defends it.

text: White's knight captures the pawn on E five. Black's knight captures the knight. White's rook captures the black knight on E five.

displayText: White gave a knight, three points, and won a pawn and a knight, four points: a gain of one point. Capturing first with the cheaper knight made that work.
text: White gave a knight, three points, and won a pawn and a knight, four points: a gain of one point. Capturing first with the cheaper knight made that work.

text: Numbers are not everything. Here one queen attacks the pawn on D five and one pawn defends it. Taking would swap White's queen, worth nine, for a single pawn.
