text: So count both armies to see who is ahead, compare what each trade gives and gets, and count attackers and defenders before every capture.

displayText: Chess players can write down every move with a short code called notation. With it, any game can be recorded, shared and played through again.
text: Chess players can write down every move with a short code called notation. With it, any game can be recorded, shared and played through again.

displayText: Notation is built on square names: the file letter, then the rank number, just as in The Chessboard lesson. These two squares are d4 and f3.
text: Notation is built on square names: the file letter, then the rank number, just as in The Chessboard lesson. These two squares are D four and F three.

displayText: Every piece apart from the pawn is written with a capital letter. The king is K, the queen is Q, the rook is R and the bishop is B.
text: Every piece apart from the pawn is written with a capital letter. The king is K, the queen is Q, the rook is R and the bishop is B.

displayText: The knight is written N, because K already stands for the king.
text: The knight is written N, because K already stands for the king.

displayText: Pawns get no letter at all. A pawn move is just the square it lands on, so White's pawn going from d2 to d4 is written d4.
text: Pawns get no letter at all. A pawn move is just the square it lands on, so White's pawn going from D two to D four is written D four.

displayText: Black answers with the knight from g8 to f6. A piece move is the piece's letter and then its new square: Nf6.
text: Black answers with the knight from G eight to F six. A piece move is the piece's letter and then its new square: N F six, meaning knight to F six.

displayText: White brings a knight out, from b1 to c3. That is Nc3.
text: White brings a knight out, from B one to C three. That is N C three.

displayText: Black's pawn steps from d7 to d5, written d5.
text: Black's pawn steps from D seven to D five, written D five.

displayText: A White move and Black's reply share one number. So far this game reads 1. d4 Nf6 2. Nc3 d5.
text: A White move and Black's reply share one number. So far this game reads: one, D four, knight F six. Two, knight C three, D five.

displayText: On move 3, White's bishop travels from c1 to g5. That is Bg5.
text: On move three, White's bishop travels from C one to G five. That is bishop G five.

displayText: Black pushes a pawn from c7 to c6, written simply c6.
text: Black pushes a pawn from C seven to C six, written simply C six.

displayText: On move 4, White's bishop takes the knight on f6. A capture puts an x before the square: Bxf6, read as bishop takes f6.
text: On move four, White's bishop takes the knight on F six. A capture puts an x before the square: B x F six, read as bishop takes F six.

displayText: Black's pawn on e7 takes the bishop back on f6. A pawn capture begins with the file the pawn left: exf6, read as e takes f6.
text: Black's pawn on E seven takes the bishop back on F six. A pawn capture begins with the file the pawn left: E x F six, read as E takes F six.

displayText: Castling has its own sign. Here the king goes from e1 to g1. Then the rook hops over it from h1 to f1. Castling on the king's side is written O-O, and said as castles kingside.
text: Castling has its own sign. Here the king goes from E one to G one. Then the rook hops over it from H one to F one. Castling on the king's side is written O O, and said as castles kingside.

displayText: On the queen's side, the king goes from e1 to c1. Then the rook hops from a1 to d1. That longer castling is written O-O-O, and said as castles queenside.
text: On the queen's side, the king goes from E one to C one. Then the rook hops from A one to D one. That longer castling is written O O O, and said as castles queenside.

displayText: Here White's rook goes from a1 to a8 and checks the black king. A checking move ends with a plus sign: Ra8+.
text: Here White's rook goes from A one to A eight and checks the black king. A checking move ends with a plus sign: rook A eight, check.

displayText: Now White's rook goes from d2 to d8, and the black king has no escape. Checkmate is marked with a hash sign: Rd8#.
text: Now White's rook goes from D two to D eight, and the black king has no escape. Checkmate is marked with a hash sign: rook D eight, checkmate.

displayText: This white pawn steps from b7 to b8 and becomes a queen. A promotion adds an equals sign and the new piece's letter: b8=Q.
text: This white pawn steps from B seven to B eight and becomes a queen. A promotion adds an equals sign and the new piece's letter: B eight equals Q, meaning it promotes to a queen.

displayText: Writers also add comments: ! after a good move and ? after a mistake. Two of them, !! or ??, mark a brilliant move or a serious blunder.
text: Writers also add comments: an exclamation mark after a good move, and a question mark after a mistake. Two exclamation marks mark a brilliant move, and two question marks a serious blunder.

displayText: Both White knights here could jump to d2, so Nd2 would not say which one went. The knight from b1 moves, so we add its file letter: Nbd2.
text: Both White knights here could jump to D two, so knight D two would not say which one went. The knight from B one moves, so we add its file letter: knight B, D two.

displayText: When the two pieces share a file, add the rank number instead. Both rooks could reach a3; the one from a1 moves, so it is written R1a3.
text: When the two pieces share a file, add the rank number instead. Both rooks could reach A three; the one from A one moves, so it is written rook one, A three.

displayText: Now you can read and write the moves of a whole game. Try writing down your next game move by move, then play it through again from the start.
text: Now you can read and write the moves of a whole game. Try writing down your next game move by move, then play it through again from the start.

displayText: Chess is played between two people. Good manners make the game pleasant for both of you, whoever wins.
text: Chess is played between two people. Good manners make the game pleasant for both of you, whoever wins.

displayText: Before the first move, greet your opponent, shake hands if that is the custom, and wish them a good game.
text: Before the first move, greet your opponent, shake hands if that is the custom, and wish them a good game.

displayText: During the game, stay quiet. Don't chat, hum, tap the table or comment on your opponent's moves.
text: During the game, stay quiet. Don't chat, hum, tap the table or comment on your opponent's moves.

displayText: Your opponent is thinking as hard as you are. Let them take their time, and keep your eyes on the board.
text: Your opponent is thinking as hard as you are. Let them take their time, and keep your eyes on the board.

displayText: Serious games use the touch-move rule. Touch one of your own pieces on purpose, and you must move it, as long as it has a legal move.
text: Serious games use the touch-move rule. Touch one of your own pieces on purpose, and you must move it, as long as it has a legal move.

displayText: So decide on your move before you reach for a piece. Here, touching the knight on g1 means the knight must move.
text: So decide on your move before you reach for a piece. Here, touching the knight on G one means the knight must move.

displayText: White pushes a pawn from c2 to c4. Black answers with a pawn from d7 to d5.
text: White pushes a pawn from C two to C four. Black answers with a pawn from D seven to D five.

displayText: The rule covers your opponent's pieces too. If White touches the pawn on d5 on purpose, White must capture it, because capturing it is legal.
text: The rule covers your opponent's pieces too. If White touches the pawn on D five on purpose, White must capture it, because capturing it is legal.

displayText: Once you let go of a piece on a legal square, the move is made and cannot be taken back. Castling is complete once the rook is placed too, and a promotion once the new piece stands on the pawn's square.
text: Once you let go of a piece on a legal square, the move is made and cannot be taken back. Castling is complete once the rook is placed too, and a promotion once the new piece stands on the pawn's square.

displayText: Sometimes a piece sits crooked on its square. On your turn, first say "I'm adjusting", or the French "j'adoube", then straighten it. That warns your opponent you are not choosing that piece to move.
text: Sometimes a piece sits crooked on its square. On your turn, first say "I'm adjusting", or the French "zhah-doob", then straighten it. That warns your opponent you are not choosing that piece to move.

displayText: Touch-move is about touching a piece on purpose. If your sleeve knocks a piece by accident, put it back, and the rule does not apply.
text: Touch-move is about touching a piece on purpose. If your sleeve knocks a piece by accident, put it back, and the rule does not apply.

displayText: If your position is hopeless, you may resign instead of playing on. Say clearly "I resign" and offer your hand.
text: If your position is hopeless, you may resign instead of playing on. Say clearly "I resign" and offer your hand.

displayText: You never have to resign. Playing on is fine while you still have chances, and games between beginners often turn around.
text: You never have to resign. Playing on is fine while you still have chances, and games between beginners often turn around.

displayText: When you win, shake hands and say "good game". Don't cheer loudly or tease your opponent.
text: When you win, shake hands and say "good game". Don't cheer loudly or tease your opponent.

displayText: When you lose, shake hands too and congratulate your opponent. Every loss teaches you something for next time.
text: When you lose, shake hands too and congratulate your opponent. Every loss teaches you something for next time.

displayText: Afterwards you might look through the game together. Do it quietly, away from anyone still playing.
text: Afterwards you might look through the game together. Do it quietly, away from anyone still playing.

displayText: Finally, set the pieces back up on their starting squares, ready for whoever plays next.
text: Finally, set the pieces back up on their starting squares, ready for whoever plays next.

displayText: Greet, stay quiet, follow touch-move, say "I'm adjusting" before straightening a piece, and be kind whether you win or lose.
text: Greet, stay quiet, follow touch-move, say "I'm adjusting" before straightening a piece, and be kind whether you win or lose.

displayText: A tournament is a competition with many players. Everyone plays several games, one in each round.
text: A tournament is a competition with many players. Everyone plays several games, one in each round.

displayText: Before each round, the organisers publish the pairings: who plays whom, on which board, and who has the white pieces.
text: Before each round, the organisers publish the pairings: who plays whom, on which board, and who has the white pieces.

displayText: A win scores one point, a draw half a point, and a loss nothing. The player with the most points at the end wins the tournament.
text: A win scores one point, a draw half a point, and a loss nothing. The player with the most points at the end wins the tournament.

displayText: Many tournaments use the Swiss system. Players are not knocked out; in each round they meet opponents with similar scores.
text: Many tournaments use the Swiss system. Players are not knocked out; in each round they meet opponents with similar scores.

displayText: Find your board and sit down before the round begins. If you arrive too late, you can lose the game without playing a move.
text: Find your board and sit down before the round begins. If you arrive too late, you can lose the game without playing a move.

displayText: Tournament games use a chess clock: two clocks joined together, one counting down your time and one counting down your opponent's.
text: Tournament games use a chess clock: two clocks joined together, one counting down your time and one counting down your opponent's.

displayText: When the game begins, White's clock is running. White opens by pushing a pawn from d2 to d4. White's clock keeps running until White presses it.
text: When the game begins, White's clock is running. White opens by pushing a pawn from D two to D four. White's clock keeps running until White presses it.

displayText: After moving, White presses the clock, which stops White's time and starts Black's. Black replies by pushing a pawn from d7 to d5, then presses the clock in turn.
text: After moving, White presses the clock, which stops White's time and starts Black's. Black replies by pushing a pawn from D seven to D five, then presses the clock in turn.

displayText: Move the piece and press the clock with the same hand. Keep your other hand away from the clock.
text: Move the piece and press the clock with the same hand. Keep your other hand away from the clock.

displayText: If your time runs out, you lose, unless your opponent could not possibly checkmate you. Then the game is a draw.
text: If your time runs out, you lose, unless your opponent could not possibly checkmate you. Then the game is a draw.

displayText: In most longer games, each player writes down every move of both sides on a scoresheet, using chess notation. In rapid games, or when very short of time, you may not have to.
text: In most longer games, each player writes down every move of both sides on a scoresheet, using chess notation. In rapid games, or when very short of time, you may not have to.

displayText: Make your move on the board first, then write it down. Here the scoresheet would show move one as d4 for White and d5 for Black.
text: Make your move on the board first, then write it down. Here the scoresheet would show move one as D four for White and D five for Black.

displayText: Every tournament has an arbiter, the referee. The arbiter makes sure the rules are followed and settles any problem.
text: Every tournament has an arbiter, the referee. The arbiter makes sure the rules are followed and settles any problem.

displayText: If something goes wrong, such as an illegal move, a faulty clock or a draw claim, pause the clock and call the arbiter. Never argue with your opponent.
text: If something goes wrong, such as an illegal move, a faulty clock or a draw claim, pause the clock and call the arbiter. Never argue with your opponent.

displayText: During play, you may not get advice from anyone, use notes or books, or analyse on another board. Check the rules on phones: they are normally not allowed with you at all, unless the event allows them, for example switched off in a bag.
text: During play, you may not get advice from anyone, use notes or books, or analyse on another board. Check the rules on phones: they are normally not allowed with you at all, unless the event allows them, for example switched off in a bag.

displayText: Walk quietly, and never talk about a game while it is being played. When you finish, leave the playing area so others can concentrate.
text: Walk quietly, and never talk about a game while it is being played. When you finish, leave the playing area so others can concentrate.

displayText: When the game ends, shake hands, both sign the scoresheets, and report the result as the organisers ask.
text: When the game ends, shake hands, both sign the scoresheets, and report the result as the organisers ask.

displayText: Check the pairings, arrive on time, press the clock with the hand you moved with, write the moves when the rules ask, and call the arbiter when you need help.
text: Check the pairings, arrive on time, press the clock with the hand you moved with, write the moves when the rules ask, and call the arbiter when you need help.

displayText: This lesson gathers every rule you have learned into one quick tour, ending with two habits to use before each move.
text: This lesson gathers every rule you have learned into one quick tour, ending with two habits to use before each move.

displayText: A pawn moves straight forward one square, or two from its starting square. It captures one square diagonally forward, so this pawn could take the knight on d3.
text: A pawn moves straight forward one square, or two from its starting square. It captures one square diagonally forward, so this pawn could take the knight on D three.

displayText: A rook moves any distance along its rank or file, as long as the path is clear.
text: A rook moves any distance along its rank or file, as long as the path is clear.

displayText: A bishop moves any distance along a diagonal, so it always stays on squares of one colour.
text: A bishop moves any distance along a diagonal, so it always stays on squares of one colour.

displayText: The queen combines rook and bishop moves: she travels any distance along a rank, a file or a diagonal.
text: The queen combines rook and bishop moves: she travels any distance along a rank, a file or a diagonal.

displayText: The knight jumps in an L shape: two squares one way, then one square to the side. In ordinary moves, it is the only piece that jumps over others.
text: The knight jumps in an L shape: two squares one way, then one square to the side. In ordinary moves, it is the only piece that jumps over others.

displayText: The king steps one square in any direction, but never onto a square that is attacked.
text: The king steps one square in any direction, but never onto a square that is attacked.

displayText: Black's king is in check from the rook on e1. A check is answered by moving the king, blocking, or capturing the checker. Here Black has only a king, so the king must move.
text: Black's king is in check from the rook on E one. A check is answered by moving the king, blocking, or capturing the checker. Here Black has only a king, so the king must move.

displayText: White's queen moves from a7 to e7, giving check. The queen covers every square around the king, and the white king guards her. That is checkmate, and White wins.
text: White's queen moves from A seven to E seven, giving check. The queen covers every square around the king, and the white king guards her. That is checkmate, and White wins.

displayText: Suppose Black is to move here. The king is not attacked, yet it has nowhere to go and Black has nothing else to move: stalemate, a draw.
text: Suppose Black is to move here. The king is not attacked, yet it has nowhere to go and Black has nothing else to move: stalemate, a draw.

displayText: White castles kingside. The king moves two squares, from e1 to g1. Then the rook goes from h1 to f1, on the king's other side.
text: White castles kingside. The king moves two squares, from E one to G one. Then the rook goes from H one to F one, on the king's other side.

displayText: Castling needs all of this: neither the king nor that rook has moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check, does not pass over an attacked square and does not finish on one.
text: Castling needs all of this: neither the king nor that rook has moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check, does not pass over an attacked square and does not finish on one.

displayText: White's pawn moves from b7 to b8 and becomes a queen. A pawn that reaches the last rank must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight.
text: White's pawn moves from B seven to B eight and becomes a queen. A pawn that reaches the last rank must become a queen, rook, bishop or knight.

displayText: Black's pawn moves two squares, from d7 to d5, and lands right beside White's pawn on e5.
text: Black's pawn moves two squares, from D seven to D five, and lands right beside White's pawn on E five.

displayText: White's pawn captures en passant, moving from e5 to d6, and the black pawn on d5 is removed. This is allowed only on the very next move.
text: White's pawn captures en passant, moving from E five to D six, and the black pawn on D five is removed. This is allowed only on the very next move.

displayText: Remember the draws: stalemate, too little material to checkmate, a position repeated three times, fifty moves each with no capture or pawn move, and agreement. Repetition and fifty moves need a claim.
text: Remember the draws: stalemate, too little material to checkmate, a position repeated three times, fifty moves each with no capture or pawn move, and agreement. Repetition and fifty moves need a claim.

displayText: Now two habits for every move. First, ask what your opponent's last move does. Does it attack one of your pieces, or threaten check?
text: Now two habits for every move. First, ask what your opponent's last move does. Does it attack one of your pieces, or threaten check?

displayText: Second, check your own move before you play it. White's knight could jump to g5, but Black's pawn on h6 attacks that square.
text: Second, check your own move before you play it. White's knight could jump to G five, but Black's pawn on H six attacks that square.

displayText: Ask both questions before every move: what is my opponent threatening, and will my piece be safe? These two habits save more games than anything else.
text: Ask both questions before every move: what is my opponent threatening, and will my piece be safe? These two habits save more games than anything else.

displayText: The opening is the first part of a game. Both sides bring their armies out, and a few simple ideas help you start well.
text: The opening is the first part of a game. Both sides bring their armies out, and a few simple ideas help you start well.

displayText: The four middle squares, d4, e4, d5 and e5, are the centre. Pawns and pieces that stand on them or aim at them have the most influence.
text: The four middle squares, D four, E four, D five and E five, are the centre. Pawns and pieces that stand on them or aim at them have the most influence.

displayText: A knight in the centre on d4 reaches eight squares. The same knight in the corner on h1 reaches only two.
text: A knight in the centre on D four reaches eight squares. The same knight in the corner on H one reaches only two.

displayText: White begins by pushing the queen's pawn two squares, to d4. It claims a centre square and lets the bishop on c1 out.
text: White begins by pushing the queen's pawn two squares, to D four. It claims a centre square and lets the bishop on C one out.

displayText: Black replies in the same way, with a pawn to d5. Each side now has a pawn in the centre.
text: Black replies in the same way, with a pawn to D five. Each side now has a pawn in the centre.

displayText: Developing means bringing a piece to a square where it does useful work. White's knight jumps to f3, where it guards d4 and watches e5.
text: Developing means bringing a piece to a square where it does useful work. White's knight jumps to F three, where it guards D four and watches E five.

displayText: Black's knight jumps to f6. It guards d5 and watches e4.
text: Black's knight jumps to F six. It guards D five and watches E four.

displayText: White's dark-squared bishop goes out to f4. Black's light-squared bishop goes out to f5.
text: White's dark-squared bishop goes out to F four. Black's light-squared bishop goes out to F five.

displayText: White's e-pawn steps forward one square, to e3. Black's e-pawn steps to e6. Both moves open a diagonal for the other bishop.
text: White's e-pawn steps forward one square, to E three. Black's e-pawn steps to E six. Both moves open a diagonal for the other bishop.

displayText: White's bishop comes to e2. Black's bishop comes to e7. Now the squares between each king and its h-rook are empty.
text: White's bishop comes to E two. Black's bishop comes to E seven. Now the squares between each king and its h-rook are empty.

displayText: White castles. The king goes two squares to g1. The rook hops over to f1.
text: White castles. The king goes two squares to G one. The rook hops over to F one.

displayText: White's king now sits behind the pawns on f2, g2 and h2, away from the busy centre. The rook on f1 is ready to join the game.
text: White's king now sits behind the pawns on F two, G two and H two, away from the busy centre. The rook on F one is ready to join the game.

displayText: Black castles as well. The king goes to g8. The rook hops over to f8.
text: Black castles as well. The king goes to G eight. The rook hops over to F eight.

displayText: Now a new game, to show what not to do. White's knight jumps to c3. Black's pawn advances to d5.
text: Now a new game, to show what not to do. White's knight jumps to C three. Black's pawn advances to D five.

displayText: White's knight jumps again, to b5. Black's c-pawn steps to c6 and attacks it.
text: White's knight jumps again, to B five. Black's c-pawn steps to C six and attacks it.

displayText: White's knight retreats to a3. Black's e-pawn advances to e5.
text: White's knight retreats to A three. Black's e-pawn advances to E five.

displayText: White has spent three moves on one knight, which now sits on the edge. Black used the same three moves to put pawns on d5 and e5.
text: White has spent three moves on one knight, which now sits on the edge. Black used the same three moves to put pawns on D five and E five.

displayText: Back to the first game, where both kings have castled. Every move there helped to claim the centre, bring out a piece or keep the king safe.
text: Back to the first game, where both kings have castled. Every move there helped to claim the centre, bring out a piece or keep the king safe.

displayText: White's second knight comes to d2. Black's second knight comes to d7.
text: White's second knight comes to D two. Black's second knight comes to D seven.

displayText: White's c-pawn steps to c3. Black's c-pawn steps to c6.
text: White's c-pawn steps to C three. Black's c-pawn steps to C six.

displayText: White's queen moves to c2. Black's queen moves to c7.
text: White's queen moves to C two. Black's queen moves to C seven.

displayText: Now nothing stands between each side's two rooks. Rooks that see each other along the back rank are connected, and they guard each other.
text: Now nothing stands between each side's two rooks. Rooks that see each other along the back rank are connected, and they guard each other.

displayText: Take the centre, develop your knights and bishops, castle early, move each piece once unless there's a good reason, and connect your rooks. Then the middle of the game can begin.
text: Take the centre, develop your knights and bishops, castle early, move each piece once unless there's a good reason, and connect your rooks. Then the middle of the game can begin.

displayText: Scholar's Mate is a quick attack in which a queen and a bishop strike together at one weak square. Many beginners fall for it, so learn it and learn to stop it.
text: Scholar's Mate is a quick attack in which a queen and a bishop strike together at one weak square. Many beginners fall for it, so learn it and learn to stop it.

displayText: At the start, Black's pawn on f7 is guarded only by Black's king. White's pawn on f2 is guarded only by White's king.
text: At the start, Black's pawn on F seven is guarded only by Black's king. White's pawn on F two is guarded only by White's king.

displayText: White's e-pawn advances to e4. Black pushes the g-pawn one square, to g6, to make room for a bishop.
text: White's e-pawn advances to E four. Black pushes the g-pawn one square, to G six, to make room for a bishop.

displayText: White's bishop goes to c4 and aims at f7. Black's bishop goes to g7.
text: White's bishop goes to C four and aims at F seven. Black's bishop goes to G seven.

displayText: White's queen comes out early, to f3. Now the queen and the bishop both aim at f7, and White threatens to take it with checkmate.
text: White's queen comes out early, to F three. Now the queen and the bishop both aim at F seven, and White threatens to take it with checkmate.

displayText: Black's knight jumps to c6. It is a useful developing move, but it does nothing about the threat to f7.
text: Black's knight jumps to C six. It is a useful developing move, but it does nothing about the threat to F seven.

displayText: White's queen captures the pawn on f7. It is checkmate.
text: White's queen captures the pawn on F seven. It is checkmate.

displayText: The king cannot take the queen, because the bishop on c4 guards her. No other black piece can reach her, and the only empty square beside the king, f8, is attacked. The game ended in four moves.
text: The king cannot take the queen, because the bishop on C four guards her. No other black piece can reach her, and the only empty square beside the king, F eight, is attacked. The game ended in four moves.

displayText: The same idea works against White's pawn on f2. Suppose White starts slowly, with a pawn to a3. Black's e-pawn advances to e5.
text: The same idea works against White's pawn on F two. Suppose White starts slowly, with a pawn to A three. Black's e-pawn advances to E five.

displayText: White pushes a pawn to h3. Black's bishop goes to c5 and aims at f2.
text: White pushes a pawn to H three. Black's bishop goes to C five and aims at F two.

displayText: White pushes a pawn to b3. Black's queen goes to f6 and aims at f2 as well.
text: White pushes a pawn to B three. Black's queen goes to F six and aims at F two as well.

displayText: White pushes a pawn to g4 and ignores the danger. Black's queen captures on f2. It is checkmate.
text: White pushes a pawn to G four and ignores the danger. Black's queen captures on F two. It is checkmate.

displayText: Back to White's attack, just after the queen came to f3. Black's pawn on f7 is attacked twice and guarded only once. Black must act now.
text: Back to White's attack, just after the queen came to F three. Black's pawn on F seven is attacked twice and guarded only once. Black must act now.

displayText: A good answer: Black's knight jumps to f6. It develops a piece and stands in the queen's way, so she no longer attacks f7.
text: A good answer: Black's knight jumps to F six. It develops a piece and stands in the queen's way, so she no longer attacks F seven.

displayText: White pushes the d-pawn to d3 to guard e4 from the knight. Black's other knight jumps to c6.
text: White pushes the d-pawn to D three to guard E four from the knight. Black's other knight jumps to C six.

displayText: White's knight goes to e2. Black's knight jumps to e5 and attacks both the queen and the bishop. A useful move that also makes a threat, so the opponent must react, is said to gain tempo.
text: White's knight goes to E two. Black's knight jumps to E five and attacks both the queen and the bishop. A useful move that also makes a threat, so the opponent must react, is said to gain tempo.

displayText: White's queen has to move again, while Black's pieces keep arriving with threats. The early queen has cost White time, and f7 is well guarded.
text: White's queen has to move again, while Black's pieces keep arriving with threats. The early queen has cost White time, and F seven is well guarded.

displayText: Back once more to the moment the queen came to f3. This time Black's e-pawn steps to e6 and cuts the bishop's line to f7.
text: Back once more to the moment the queen came to F three. This time Black's e-pawn steps to E six and cuts the bishop's line to F seven.

displayText: Now only the queen attacks f7, and the king guards it. If the queen captured there, the king would simply capture her.
text: Now only the queen attacks F seven, and the king guards it. If the queen captured there, the king would simply capture her.

displayText: An early queen attack looks frightening, but it is easy to meet. Guard f7, keep developing, and chase the queen with your pieces when you can.
text: An early queen attack looks frightening, but it is easy to meet. Guard F seven, keep developing, and chase the queen with your pieces when you can.

displayText: Now try it yourself against the computer. Here Black threatens checkmate on f2. Stop the threat with a developing move, castle, and then chase Black's queen.
text: Now try it yourself against the computer. Here Black threatens checkmate on F two. Stop the threat with a developing move, castle, and then chase Black's queen.

displayText: A fork is one piece attacking two enemy pieces at the same time. The opponent can usually save only one of them.
text: A fork is one piece attacking two enemy pieces at the same time. The opponent can usually save only one of them.

displayText: Knights are the champions of the fork. A knight's jump cannot be blocked, and its L-shaped attacks are easy for the opponent to overlook.
text: Knights are the champions of the fork. A knight's jump cannot be blocked, and its L-shaped attacks are easy for the opponent to overlook.

displayText: White's knight lands on e7. It checks the king on g8 and attacks the rook on c8 at the same moment.
text: White's knight lands on E seven. It checks the king on G eight and attacks the rook on C eight at the same moment.

displayText: Black has to deal with the check first. The king steps into the corner, to h8.
text: Black has to deal with the check first. The king steps into the corner, to H eight.

displayText: White's knight captures the rook on c8. One move made two threats, and a whole rook was won.
text: White's knight captures the rook on C eight. One move made two threats, and a whole rook was won.

displayText: Pawns can fork as well. Black's knights stand on d6 and f6, with one empty square between them.
text: Pawns can fork as well. Black's knights stand on D six and F six, with one empty square between them.

displayText: White's pawn advances to e5, right between them. It attacks both knights at once.
text: White's pawn advances to E five, right between them. It attacks both knights at once.

displayText: Neither knight can capture the pawn, and Black can move only one of them. White will capture the other one. Even if Black wins the pawn back, White has gained a knight, worth three, for a pawn, worth one.
text: Neither knight can capture the pawn, and Black can move only one of them. White will capture the other one. Even if Black wins the pawn back, White has gained a knight, worth three, for a pawn, worth one.

displayText: The queen moves in every direction, so she forks often. Look at Black's king on g8 and the rook on a8.
text: The queen moves in every direction, so she forks often. Look at Black's king on G eight and the rook on A eight.

displayText: White's queen goes to d5. She checks the king along one diagonal and attacks the rook along another.
text: White's queen goes to D five. She checks the king along one diagonal and attacks the rook along another.

displayText: Black's king slips into the corner, to h8. White's queen takes the rook on a8, giving check again.
text: Black's king slips into the corner, to H eight. White's queen takes the rook on A eight, giving check again.

displayText: A fork works best when the forking piece cannot simply be captured. Before you fork, check that the square you land on is safe.
text: A fork works best when the forking piece cannot simply be captured. Before you fork, check that the square you land on is safe.

displayText: A fork that includes a check is usually the strongest kind. Unless the forking piece can simply be taken, the opponent is busy with the check and cannot rescue the second target.
text: A fork that includes a check is usually the strongest kind. Unless the forking piece can simply be taken, the opponent is busy with the check and cannot rescue the second target.

displayText: Before each move, ask: can one of my pieces attack two valuable targets at once? Kings, queens and rooks make the best targets.
text: Before each move, ask: can one of my pieces attack two valuable targets at once? Kings, queens and rooks make the best targets.

displayText: Now try it yourself against the computer. White's knight on g5 can fork two of Black's pieces. Find the fork, win material, and play on to win the game.
text: Now try it yourself against the computer. White's knight on G five can fork two of Black's pieces. Find the fork, win material, and play on to win the game.

displayText: A pin is an attack on a piece that cannot move off its line, or should not, because a more valuable piece stands behind it on the same line.
text: A pin is an attack on a piece that cannot move off its line, or should not, because a more valuable piece stands behind it on the same line.

displayText: White's bishop goes to b5 and attacks the knight on c6. Behind that knight, on the same diagonal, is Black's king on e8.
text: White's bishop goes to B five and attacks the knight on C six. Behind that knight, on the same diagonal, is Black's king on E eight.

displayText: If this knight stepped away, the bishop would be giving check, and the rules forbid that. A knight can never stay on its line, so this one is frozen.
text: If this knight stepped away, the bishop would be giving check, and the rules forbid that. A knight can never stay on its line, so this one is frozen.

displayText: A pin against the king is called an absolute pin. The rules forbid the pinned piece to step off the line; at most it may slide along it or capture the pinner.
text: A pin against the king is called an absolute pin. The rules forbid the pinned piece to step off the line; at most it may slide along it or capture the pinner.

displayText: Now use the pin. White's pawn advances to d5 and attacks the knight. The knight cannot run, so White will capture it next move.
text: Now use the pin. White's pawn advances to D five and attacks the knight. The knight cannot run, so White will capture it next move.

displayText: Here White's bishop on g5 attacks the knight on f6. Behind the knight, on the same diagonal, stands Black's queen on d8.
text: Here White's bishop on G five attacks the knight on F six. Behind the knight, on the same diagonal, stands Black's queen on D eight.

displayText: The rules let this knight move, since no king hides behind it. Yet moving it hands the queen to the bishop. We call this a relative pin: legal to move, but very costly.
text: The rules let this knight move, since no king hides behind it. Yet moving it hands the queen to the bishop. We call this a relative pin: legal to move, but very costly.

displayText: White's pawn advances to e5 and attacks the pinned knight. If the knight moves, the queen falls; if it stays, the pawn takes it.
text: White's pawn advances to E five and attacks the pinned knight. If the knight moves, the queen falls; if it stays, the pawn takes it.

displayText: Black cannot keep both the knight and the queen. A pinned piece attacked by a pawn is very often simply lost.
text: Black cannot keep both the knight and the queen. A pinned piece attacked by a pawn is very often simply lost.

displayText: Rooks and queens pin along files and ranks. Here White's rook on e1 pins Black's bishop on e6 to the king on e8.
text: Rooks and queens pin along files and ranks. Here White's rook on E one pins Black's bishop on E six to the king on E eight.

displayText: Only bishops, rooks and queens can pin, because they attack along lines. A knight, a pawn or a king cannot pin anything.
text: Only bishops, rooks and queens can pin, because they attack along lines. A knight, a pawn or a king cannot pin anything.

displayText: Look for two enemy pieces on the same line, with the more valuable one behind. A bishop, rook or queen on that line can pin the front piece.
text: Look for two enemy pieces on the same line, with the more valuable one behind. A bishop, rook or queen on that line can pin the front piece.

displayText: When you pin a piece, attack it again, ideally with a pawn. Also check what the pinned piece was guarding, because it may no longer be able to help.
text: When you pin a piece, attack it again, ideally with a pawn. Also check what the pinned piece was guarding, because it may no longer be able to help.

displayText: Now try it yourself against the computer. Black's knight on c6 stands on the same diagonal as Black's king. Pin it, attack it, and win material.
text: Now try it yourself against the computer. Black's knight on C six stands on the same diagonal as Black's king. Pin it, attack it, and win material.

displayText: A skewer is an attack on a valuable piece that has to move away, so that a piece behind it can be captured.
text: A skewer is an attack on a valuable piece that has to move away, so that a piece behind it can be captured.

displayText: White's rook slides to e2. It checks the king on e5, and behind the king, on the same file, stands Black's queen on e8.
text: White's rook slides to E two. It checks the king on E five, and behind the king, on the same file, stands Black's queen on E eight.

displayText: Black must get out of check. Nothing can block the line or capture the rook, so the king has to step off the file.
text: Black must get out of check. Nothing can block the line or capture the rook, so the king has to step off the file.

displayText: Black's king steps aside, to f5.
text: Black's king steps aside, to F five.

displayText: White's rook captures the queen on e8. The skewer won a queen for nothing.
text: White's rook captures the queen on E eight. The skewer won a queen for nothing.

displayText: Think of a skewer as a pin turned round. A pin traps a cheaper piece with a dearer one behind it. A skewer hits the dearer piece first, and it has to get out of the way.
text: Think of a skewer as a pin turned round. A pin traps a cheaper piece with a dearer one behind it. A skewer hits the dearer piece first, and it has to get out of the way.

displayText: Bishops skewer along diagonals. Black's king stands on f5, and further along the same diagonal is Black's rook on h7.
text: Bishops skewer along diagonals. Black's king stands on F five, and further along the same diagonal is Black's rook on H seven.

displayText: White's bishop goes to d3 and checks the king. The rook on h7 is behind the king on the same diagonal.
text: White's bishop goes to D three and checks the king. The rook on H seven is behind the king on the same diagonal.

displayText: Black's king steps aside, to e5. White's bishop takes the rook on h7.
text: Black's king steps aside, to E five. White's bishop takes the rook on H seven.

displayText: A skewer does not need a king. Here Black's queen stands on d4, and the rook on h8 is behind her on the long diagonal.
text: A skewer does not need a king. Here Black's queen stands on D four, and the rook on H eight is behind her on the long diagonal.

displayText: White's bishop goes to b2 and attacks the queen. If the queen takes the bishop, White's rook on b1 takes her back.
text: White's bishop goes to B two and attacks the queen. If the queen takes the bishop, White's rook on B one takes her back.

displayText: Black's queen escapes to d5. White's bishop takes the rook on h8.
text: Black's queen escapes to D five. White's bishop takes the rook on H eight.

displayText: Only bishops, rooks and queens can skewer, because they attack along lines. A knight, a pawn or a king cannot.
text: Only bishops, rooks and queens can skewer, because they attack along lines. A knight, a pawn or a king cannot.

displayText: Look for two enemy pieces on one line with the more valuable one in front, especially the king. Attack the front piece, and the one behind may fall.
text: Look for two enemy pieces on one line with the more valuable one in front, especially the king. Attack the front piece, and the one behind may fall.

displayText: Now try it yourself against the computer. Black's king on e6 and queen on g8 stand on the same diagonal. Find the skewer and win the queen.
text: Now try it yourself against the computer. Black's king on E six and queen on G eight stand on the same diagonal. Find the skewer and win the queen.

displayText: Sometimes the piece that moves is not the piece that attacks. When it steps aside, it uncovers an attack by a piece standing behind it. This is a discovered attack.
text: Sometimes the piece that moves is not the piece that attacks. When it steps aside, it uncovers an attack by a piece standing behind it. This is a discovered attack.

displayText: White's rook on d1 points up the d-file towards Black's queen on d7. But White's own bishop on d3 stands in between, so for now the rook's attack is blocked.
text: White's rook on D one points up the d-file towards Black's queen on D seven. But White's own bishop on D three stands in between, so for now the rook's attack is blocked.

displayText: The bishop steps from d3 to e2. Now nothing stands between the rook and the queen: the rook's attack has been uncovered.
text: The bishop steps from D three to E two. Now nothing stands between the rook and the queen: the rook's attack has been uncovered.

displayText: A single threat like this is easy to meet: Black's queen can simply step to safety. To win something, the piece that moves should make a threat of its own.
text: A single threat like this is easy to meet: Black's queen can simply step to safety. To win something, the piece that moves should make a threat of its own.

displayText: Back to the start. This time the bishop takes the pawn on h7 and gives check to Black's king. At the same moment, the rook's attack on the queen is uncovered.
text: Back to the start. This time the bishop takes the pawn on H seven and gives check to Black's king. At the same moment, the rook's attack on the queen is uncovered.

displayText: Black must answer the check first. Black's king takes the bishop on h7. Then White's rook takes the queen on d7.
text: Black must answer the check first. Black's king takes the bishop on H seven. Then White's rook takes the queen on D seven.

displayText: White gave a bishop, worth three, and won the queen, worth nine. The check meant Black had no time to save the queen.
text: White gave a bishop, worth three, and won the queen, worth nine. The check meant Black had no time to save the queen.

displayText: Here White's bishop on b2 aims along the long diagonal towards Black's rook on h8. White's own knight on d4 is in the way.
text: Here White's bishop on B two aims along the long diagonal towards Black's rook on H eight. White's own knight on D four is in the way.

displayText: The knight jumps from d4 to b5 and attacks Black's queen on c7. The same jump uncovers the bishop's attack on the rook.
text: The knight jumps from D four to B five and attacks Black's queen on C seven. The same jump uncovers the bishop's attack on the rook.

displayText: Black has one move and two pieces under attack. If the queen escapes, the bishop takes the rook, so White wins material either way.
text: Black has one move and two pieces under attack. If the queen escapes, the bishop takes the rook, so White wins material either way.

displayText: The most dangerous discovered attack uncovers a check. White's rook on e1 aims at Black's king on e8, with White's knight on e5 in between.
text: The most dangerous discovered attack uncovers a check. White's rook on E one aims at Black's king on E eight, with White's knight on E five in between.

displayText: The knight jumps from e5 to c4 and attacks the queen on b6. Its jump uncovers the rook's check on Black's king.
text: The knight jumps from E five to C four and attacks the queen on B six. Its jump uncovers the rook's check on Black's king.

displayText: Black has to answer the check, and every answer still loses the queen. Black's king steps to f8. White's knight takes the queen on b6.
text: Black has to answer the check, and every answer still loses the queen. Black's king steps to F eight. White's knight takes the queen on B six.

displayText: Here the knight jumps from e4 to d6 and gives check itself, while it also uncovers the rook's check. Two pieces check the king at once: a double check.
text: Here the knight jumps from E four to D six and gives check itself, while it also uncovers the rook's check. Two pieces check the king at once: a double check.

displayText: Black cannot block two lines or capture two pieces in one move. Against a double check, only a king move helps. The knight on d6 also attacks Black's queen on b5.
text: Black cannot block two lines or capture two pieces in one move. Against a double check, only a king move helps. The knight on D six also attacks Black's queen on B five.

displayText: Black's king steps to d8. White's knight takes the queen on b5.
text: Black's king steps to D eight. White's knight takes the queen on B five.

displayText: To find these chances, look for your rook, bishop or queen lined up behind one of your own pieces, pointing at an enemy king or a valuable piece.
text: To find these chances, look for your rook, bishop or queen lined up behind one of your own pieces, pointing at an enemy king or a valuable piece.

displayText: The same trick can be played against you. When an enemy piece stands in front of their own rook, bishop or queen, ask what it would uncover if it moved.
text: The same trick can be played against you. When an enemy piece stands in front of their own rook, bishop or queen, ask what it would uncover if it moved.

displayText: Now you can try it yourself. White's knight on e5 stands between White's rook and Black's king. Find a knight move that uncovers check and wins something.
text: Now you can try it yourself. White's knight on E five stands between White's rook and Black's king. Find a knight move that uncovers check and wins something.

displayText: A guarded piece is hard to win. But if you remove the piece that guards it, the target is left alone. This idea is called removing the defender.
text: A guarded piece is hard to win. But if you remove the piece that guards it, the target is left alone. This idea is called removing the defender.

displayText: White's rook on e1 attacks Black's bishop on e5. Black's knight on c6 guards that bishop.

displayText: If the rook took the bishop now, the knight would take the rook. White would give a rook, worth five, for a bishop, worth three.
